task_row_model.query: How can I implement an efficient, thread-safe LRU cache in Python that supports both synchronous and asynchronous usage, guarantees O(1) get/put operations, performs eviction safely, and avoids deadlocks when accessed concurrently from threads and asyncio tasks?

documents.content: A common synchronous approach to LRU caches in Python uses collections.OrderedDict: on a put, move_to_end(key) and popitem(last=False) to evict the least-recently-used entry. For thread safety wrap all public methods with a single threading.Lock or threading.RLock so state updates (dict and order) are atomic. This yields amortized O(1) get and put because OrderedDict operations are constant time. However, this pattern does not address asyncio: awaiting while holding a threading lock can block the event loop or cause lock inversion if an async wrapper also acquires an asyncio.Lock. Use only for purely synchronous programs.

Design for O(1) operations: maintain a dict mapping keys to nodes and a doubly linked list of nodes representing recency; on get, move node to head; on put, insert or move then evict tail if capacity exceeded. For safe concurrent access, protect the core data structure with a single threading.RLock and implement all mutation logic under that lock. To support async callers without deadlocks, provide async wrappers that call the synchronous methods via loop.run_in_executor so the event loop never awaits while holding a threading lock. Eviction must run inside the locked critical section. For higher concurrency, consider sharding the cache into multiple segments with independent locks.

Asyncio concurrency requires avoiding blocking the event loop. Use asyncio.Lock or ensure long-running or blocking code runs in an executor with loop.run_in_executor. Never await while holding a blocking threading.Lock: that combination can produce deadlocks if a thread tries to acquire the threading.Lock while awaiting tasks hold an asyncio.Lock. One strategy is to keep a single-threaded core protected by a threading.Lock and expose async wrappers that offload to an executor, or design entirely non-blocking algorithms using asyncio primitives only. Careful ordering of lock acquisition and minimizing critical-section time reduces the likelihood of deadlocks.

Distributed caching and TTL-based eviction use different trade-offs than LRU. Systems that require horizontal scaling often use consistent hashing and per-node TTLs or approximate frequency counters for LFU; these approaches accept eventual eviction rather than strict recency guarantees. LFU uses counters and sometimes periodic decay to prevent cache pollution by old hot items. Such designs focus on network partition tolerance, replication, and stale data, and rely on asynchronous background processes to clean entries. While relevant for large-scale caching, they do not provide constant-time local LRU semantics or straightforward thread/async interoperability for a single-process in-memory cache.

functools.lru_cache is a decorator that provides memoization for pure functions, automatically evicting least-recently-used results when maxsize is reached. It uses a dict and a linked list internally to achieve O(1) operations for cache hits and insertions. The decorator is convenient but limited: it only works with hashable function arguments, does not expose eviction hooks, and in CPython its cache is not designed for mixed sync/async use. For fine-grained control, capacity tuning, or explicit thread-safe semantics across classes or coroutine interfaces, a custom cache implementation is usually required.
